title: The real risk of AI: we stop trying
gist: In an interview about her book 'We Are Not Machines,' FT columnist Sarah O'Connor argues that AI's real damage to work so far comes less from job elimination than from degraded quality and workers reduced to being the 'human-in-the-loop' patch for imperfect automation — and that whether AI adoption goes well or badly hinges on whether workers have bargaining power over how it's deployed, not on the technology itself.

themes.theme: AI degrading quality in white-collar creative work: translation

insights.claim: Translation agencies now use a 'Machine Translation Post-Editing' model in which subtitles are run through AI first, then human translators are paid to check and 'humanize' the output — but at roughly twice the pace for half the price of translating from scratch, which agencies expect translators to absorb to maintain their income.
insights.speaker: Sarah O'Connor
insights.so_what: A concrete, replicable business model pattern (AI-first, human-cleanup, at higher throughput/lower per-unit pay) worth watching across other white-collar services being restructured around AI, including localization and content-vendor pricing models.
insights.quote: The problem is that the agency expects translators to do this at twice the pace for half the price
insights.locator: Answer on the translator Petr

insights.claim: A Swedish study comparing the full corpus of subtitles for a TV show before and after the introduction of Machine Translation Post-Editing found quality declined across every measured metric, with more errors and thinner language that failed to reflect the richness of the original dialogue.
insights.speaker: Sarah O'Connor
insights.so_what: Rare empirical, corpus-level evidence of measurable AI-driven quality erosion in a specific creative-service niche — a template study for benchmarking quality degradation claims in other AI-augmented white-collar work (e.g., legal drafting, journalism, customer support).
insights.quote: There was a big study in Sweden recently, which compared the whole corpus of subtitles for a particular TV show, before and after the introduction of this Machine Translation Post-Editing system.
insights.locator: Answer on the Luddite parallel

insights.claim: Translators report that having AI-generated output already on the page makes it psychologically harder to think creatively from scratch, turning a formerly creative role into something faster but more mechanical and 'production-line' — the precise opposite of AI's promise to free workers for the creative parts of their jobs.
insights.speaker: Sarah O'Connor
insights.so_what: A specific psychological/workflow mechanism (anchoring on an existing AI draft suppresses creative reframing) that explains why AI augmentation can reduce rather than enhance output quality even when workers retain final editorial control.
insights.quote: a lot of translators have said that it’s very hard to be creative in your own solutions if you’ve got a solution sitting in front of you. It’s difficult to think from scratch about a different way of doing things.
insights.locator: Answer on the translator Petr

themes.theme: AI-detection arms race and the 'humanizer' problem

insights.claim: A biotech-company copywriter had her human-written articles flagged as AI-generated by an AI-detection tool after Google rankings of the company's webpages dropped; when she fed her manager's own live spoken words into the same detector, it also scored as substantially AI-written, exposing the detector's unreliability.
insights.speaker: Sarah O'Connor
insights.so_what: A vivid, verifiable illustration of AI-content-detector false positives affecting real SEO/ranking decisions — relevant to evaluating the reliability of AI-detection tools now embedded in content-marketing and search-ranking workflows.
insights.quote: she sat while he was talking and typed out what he was saying in real-time, then turned her screen to him and put what he had just said into the same AI detector. It came back as substantially AI-written.
insights.locator: Answer on the copywriter and the 'humanizer' tool

insights.claim: The prescribed fix for content flagged as AI-written was to run it through a second AI tool called a 'humanizer,' which paradoxically made the writing worse by introducing spelling mistakes and grammar errors rather than restoring genuine human quality.
insights.speaker: Sarah O'Connor
insights.so_what: Documents a self-defeating AI-tooling loop (AI-detector flags human content, a second AI tool 'fixes' it by degrading it) with direct relevance to the content-marketing/SEO tool vendor ecosystem and to Google's AI-content ranking signals.
insights.quote: what she found really depressing was that the humanizer made the language worse, adding spelling mistakes, grammar errors and just deforming it really.
insights.locator: Answer on the copywriter and the 'humanizer' tool

insights.claim: O'Connor herself deleted a line from her own book's conclusion because, on rereading, it matched an overused AI-generated sentence structure she'd become sensitized to after a year immersed in AI content online — illustrating how pervasive AI writing patterns are now reshaping stylistic choices even among professional human writers.
insights.speaker: Sarah O'Connor
insights.so_what: A first-person example of AI-style saturation creating a chilling effect on human writers' natural stylistic choices, relevant to assessing how AI-content ubiquity is altering professional writing norms broadly.
insights.quote: having spent the last year immersed in AI slop on places like LinkedIn, I thought to myself, oh God, that sounds like something ChatGPT or Claude would write.
insights.locator: Answer on the copywriter and the 'humanizer' tool

themes.theme: Creative jobs are more exposed than expected, physical jobs less so

insights.claim: A decade ago it was widely assumed creative jobs would be shielded from automation while physical/manual jobs would be automated first; instead, building machines that perform basic physical tasks has proven surprisingly difficult, while machines mimicking human cognition and creativity have advanced startlingly fast — making creative professions among the more vulnerable ones.
insights.speaker: Sarah O'Connor
insights.so_what: A high-conviction reversal of a decade-old consensus assumption — directly relevant to reassessing valuation premia on 'AI-proof' creative-services and physical-labor-heavy businesses, since the expected automation-exposure ranking has flipped.
insights.quote: Sadly, I do think they are among the more vulnerable ones, despite the fact that demand for human-created stuff – whether it’s music, novels, performances, film – is still strong.
insights.locator: Answer on whether creative jobs are the most vulnerable

insights.claim: As AI content becomes harder to distinguish from human work, proving the provenance of creative output will become increasingly difficult for freelance creators trying to find a market; nascent 'human-made' labelling schemes (modeled on fair-trade certification) are unlikely to work because there is no consensus on how much AI use disqualifies a work as human-made.
insights.speaker: Sarah O'Connor
insights.so_what: Flags provenance/authenticity verification as a structural, unresolved market problem for creative-content platforms and marketplaces — relevant to any 'proof of human origin' certification or labeling business model.
insights.quote: There have been people coming up with labelling schemes for a ‘human-created’ product, a bit like fair-trade but for humans versus AI, though I’m sceptical that will work because it’s such a grey area.
insights.locator: Answer on whether creative jobs are the most vulnerable

insights.claim: In Hollywood, AI is not replacing scriptwriting or actors directly, but is compressing costs and speeding up mid-value-chain production roles such as special effects and storyboarding — a bifurcated pattern where ideation stays human but production-process labor is squeezed.
insights.speaker: Sarah O'Connor
insights.so_what: A specific exposure map for entertainment-industry labor and cost structure — useful for assessing margin and headcount implications for studios and production-services vendors.
insights.quote: lots of jobs are primed for some form of automation, with incentives for employers at the top to compress costs and increase speed. We’re starting to see this in Hollywood.
insights.locator: Answer on whether creative jobs are the most vulnerable

themes.theme: The Luddite parallel: quality, not technology, was always the real complaint

insights.claim: The Luddites did not object to new technology itself; they objected to machines and deskilled labor producing objectively lower-quality goods — such as 'cut-ups' stockings stitched from cut cloth pieces that fell apart, versus the robust one-piece knitting method they had used — that dragged their trade into disrepute.
insights.speaker: Sarah O'Connor
insights.so_what: Reframes the 'Luddite' label away from blanket anti-technology sentiment toward a specific, still-relevant grievance about quality degradation from deskilling — directly parallels the translation-industry quality-decline data point.
insights.quote: The Luddites argued that these were terrible quality, would fall apart after they’d been worn a few times and were dragging their trade into disrepute.
insights.locator: Answer on the Luddite parallel

insights.claim: O'Connor's own experience rediscovering the audio quality of her childhood CD player versus compressed Spotify streaming illustrates how consumers can accept a quality-for-convenience trade-off without consciously realizing they made it — a dynamic she fears could apply to prose or music increasingly shaped by AI.
insights.speaker: Sarah O'Connor
insights.so_what: A useful consumer-behavior metaphor for 'silent' quality degradation being accepted en masse — relevant to thinking about how AI-generated content could normalize lower quality bars across media without triggering visible backlash.
insights.quote: I did some research and realised that makes sense because on Spotify, particularly the free version, the quality of the sound is terrible.
insights.locator: Answer on the Luddite parallel

themes.theme: What separates good AI adoption from bad: worker control and bargaining power

insights.claim: O'Connor's central finding is that whether AI adoption feels positive or negative to workers depends less on the technology itself than on whether workers feel the machines are working for them, versus feeling they are working for the machines as the 'human-in-the-loop' patching gaps in imperfect automated systems.
insights.speaker: Sarah O'Connor
insights.so_what: The book's central actionable framework for evaluating any company's AI rollout: worker agency/control over deployment is a better predictor of successful adoption (and by extension productivity, retention, quality) than the sophistication of the technology itself.
insights.quote: ‘do you feel that these machines are working for you or do you feel that you are working for the machines?’
insights.locator: Answer on workers having control over new tools

insights.claim: In Sweden, a 'co-determination' system requires employers to negotiate with workers before deploying workplace technology; miners overseeing autonomous trucks and loaders via remote control rooms reported feeling in control and positive about the change, unlike Amazon warehouse workers or translators forced to match machine-set pace.
insights.speaker: Sarah O'Connor
insights.so_what: A concrete institutional mechanism (mandatory pre-deployment worker negotiation) correlated with positive AI-adoption outcomes — relevant to assessing labor-relations and retention risk for companies rolling out automation without similar consultation structures.
insights.quote: When technology enters the workplace, and an employer wants to do something with it that will change the nature of the job, they have to sit down with the workers and negotiate over it first.
insights.locator: Answer on workers having control over new tools

insights.claim: The Writers Guild of America, anticipating AI's impact just as ChatGPT emerged before its next round of studio contract negotiations, went on strike in 2023 (joined by actors) and secured an agreement giving writers the right to decide when and how AI is used, explicitly barring studios from using AI purely as a cost-cutting measure.
insights.speaker: Sarah O'Connor
insights.so_what: A concrete, negotiated template for labor-side AI governance in a unionized creative industry — a reference case for assessing collective-bargaining risk/opportunity in other AI-exposed unionized sectors, though note production has still shifted to lower-cost locations outside LA regardless.
insights.quote: We can use AI but we don’t have to, so we will be the ones that get to decide when and how to use it. And anything that we create, has to be rewarded as such,
insights.locator: Answer on the Hollywood writers

insights.claim: The Writers Guild's negotiating strategy was to secure AI protections early, 'while the technology is still nowhere near as good as you' — a bargaining-power principle O'Connor holds up as a model for other professions facing AI disruption.
insights.speaker: Sarah O'Connor
insights.so_what: A generalizable negotiating-timing principle: labor groups gain more leverage by negotiating AI terms before the technology matures enough to threaten their jobs outright, not after.
insights.quote: if you do have bargaining power, it makes sense to negotiate early while the technology is still nowhere near as good as you
insights.locator: Answer on the Hollywood writers

themes.theme: Workers are not passive: anticipatory labour market decisions

insights.claim: O'Connor argues workers are not passive victims of technological disruption but make 'anticipatory labour market decisions' ahead of it — citing the historical example of horse-drawn teamsters, whose profession aged as younger workers avoided entering it once motorized trucks became foreseeable around the turn of the 20th century, even before trucks became widespread after WWI.
insights.speaker: Sarah O'Connor
insights.so_what: A historical framework for forecasting labor-supply shifts in AI-exposed professions today by watching university enrollment and career-choice trends as a leading indicator, ahead of actual job losses materializing.
insights.quote: the writing seemed to be on the wall and the profession got older because younger people decided to go elsewhere. We’re seeing this in the kinds of subjects that young people are choosing to do at university now.
insights.locator: Answer on which interviewees were reassuring

themes.theme: The book's central warning: humans retreating, not machines advancing

insights.claim: O'Connor's core fear, stated as the book's central thesis, is that machines will achieve human-like capability not primarily through their own technological progress but because humans retreat from using their own faculties and stop trying — 'that's how the machines catch up with us.'
insights.speaker: Sarah O'Connor
insights.so_what: The article's headline thesis and single most important framing: the AI risk to guard against is behavioral/social (human skill atrophy and reduced effort) rather than purely technological, which shifts the locus of mitigation toward labor and education policy rather than AI capability regulation alone.
insights.quote: we could retreat into a worse, more needy version of ourselves. This is my biggest fear, I think, that as humans we will just retreat, and that’s how the machines catch up with us.
insights.locator: Answer on machines achieving human-like intelligence

insights.claim: Multiple translators independently told O'Connor that everyday human language — both spoken and written — is becoming flatter and more machine-like, because people are absorbing so much AI-generated copy that they are starting to imitate it.
insights.speaker: Sarah O'Connor
insights.so_what: A linguistic-homogenization signal worth monitoring — if human writing style is converging toward AI-typical patterns at scale, this affects everything from marketing copy differentiation to future AI-detection reliability.
insights.quote: A number of the translators that I spoke to said to me completely independently that they’ve noticed the language that people use in general with each other, or their written language, is becoming a bit flatter and more machine-like
insights.locator: Answer on machines achieving human-like intelligence

insights.claim: O'Connor foresees a plausible future in which many people prefer AI companions — available 24/7, infinitely patient, undemanding — over the 'messy imperfections' of real human relationships, which could erode people's tolerance for the give-and-take required in genuine human relationships.
insights.speaker: Sarah O'Connor
insights.so_what: A specific, named risk relevant to evaluating AI-companion app products (e.g., Character.AI-style services) — not just their commercial upside but their potential social/relational externalities.
insights.quote: I can see a plausible future where a lot of people start to prefer the company of AI companions because they’re available 24/7, they have endless patience, they don’t need anything for themselves
insights.locator: Answer on machines achieving human-like intelligence

themes.theme: Regulation, rhetoric and the case for active intervention

insights.claim: O'Connor criticizes 'tsunami' metaphors commonly used in AI discourse as rhetoric useful to tech companies seeking to resist regulation, because framing disruption as an unstoppable natural force makes workers and society feel powerless to act.
insights.speaker: Sarah O'Connor
insights.so_what: A media-literacy framework for discounting industry-favored 'inevitability' narratives around AI disruption when evaluating regulatory or labor-policy debates.
insights.quote: You scrutinise the use of tsunami metaphors in discussions about AI, pointing out that this is useful language for tech companies hoping to resist regulation because it leaves us feeling powerless.
insights.locator: Question framing on tsunami metaphors

insights.claim: O'Connor argues that, as with the Industrial Revolution, technology alone never automatically distributes its productivity gains fairly — it required organized labor unions and legislative action (workplace safety rules, the end of child labor) to ensure broad-based benefit, and society must actively repeat that effort for the current AI transition.
insights.speaker: Sarah O'Connor
insights.so_what: A policy-relevant historical framework arguing that positive AI-era labor outcomes require deliberate collective action (unionization, regulation) rather than emerging automatically from market forces — directly relevant to labor-policy and AI-regulation debates.
insights.quote: Generations of workers formed trade unions to make sure that workers got a fairer share of the productivity gains, and parliamentarians fought for protections on health and safety and the end of child labour.
insights.locator: Final answer on the book's takeaway message
